title: Question 12
stem:
One nuclear reaction that can take place in a nuclear reactor may be represented, in part, by the equation
$$^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow ^{95}_{42}\text{Mo} + ^{139}_{57}\text{La} + 2^{1}_{0}\text{n} + ............ + \text{energy}$$
Data for a nucleus and some particles are given in Fig. 12.1.
{{figure:figure_12_1}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Complete the nuclear reaction shown above.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the total top numbers and total bottom numbers on the left and right sides separately. The top numbers already balance, so focus on what is missing to balance the bottom numbers.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Check What Is Already Balanced**
Think of the top number as nucleon count and the bottom number as charge count. Both must stay the same from left to right. On the left you have $235+1 = 236$ nucleons and $92+0 = 92$ units of charge.

Step 2: **Balance the Charge**
On the right so far: nucleons $95+139+2\times 1 = 236$, which already matches. Charge is $42+57+2\times 0 = 99$, which is 7 too high. Each $^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$ adds 0 to the top and $-1$ to the bottom, so you need 7 of them: $$92 = 42 + 57 + 7\times(-1)$$ That gives $7\,^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Show that the energy equivalent to $1.00\text{ u}$ is $934\text{ MeV}$.

markscheme_points.text: $= 1.494 \times 10^{-10}$ J division by $1.60 \times 10^{-13}$ clear to give 934 MeV

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking which famous Einstein relation links a small amount of mass to a large amount of energy, and recall the mass of $1.00\text{ u}$ in $\text{kg}$.
Hint 2: Calculate the energy in joules first using $c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, then think how to change joules into electronvolts.
Hint 3: Remember $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ so $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, and divide your joule answer by this to reach MeV.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Turn Mass Into Energy in Joules**
Mass and energy are the same thing in different forms. With $m = 1.00\text{ u} = 1.66\times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$: $$E = mc^2$$ $$E = (1.66\times 10^{-27})\times (3.00\times 10^8)^2$$ $$E \approx 1.49\times 10^{-10}\text{ J}$$ This is tiny in joules because one atom is so light.

Step 2: **Convert Joules to MeV**
Nuclear energies are much easier in MeV. Since $1\text{ eV} = 1.60\times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$: $$1\text{ MeV} = 1.60\times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$$ $$E = \frac{1.494\times 10^{-10}}{1.60\times 10^{-13}}\text{ MeV}$$ $$E \approx 934\text{ MeV}$$ So $1.00\text{ u}$ is equivalent to about $934\text{ MeV}$, as required.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of lanthanum-139 ($^{139}_{57}\text{La}$).
hints: Hint 1: Think of the La-139 nucleus as built from separate protons and neutrons. Count how many of each it contains from $^{139}_{57}\text{La}$.
Hint 2: Find the difference between the total mass of those separate protons plus neutrons and the actual given nuclear mass of 138.955 u. This missing mass is the mass defect.
Hint 3: Change that mass defect in u into energy in MeV using your result from (b)(i), then remember to share it equally among all 139 nucleons.
parts.proper_answer: Mass defect $\approx 1.17\text{ u}$, total binding energy $\approx 1090\text{ MeV}$, binding energy per nucleon $\approx 7.85\text{ MeV}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Mass Defect**
$^{139}_{57}\text{La}$ has $Z = 57$ protons and $A-Z = 139-57 = 82$ neutrons. Add their separate masses and subtract the bound nucleus mass: $$\Delta m = Z m_p + (A-Z)m_n - m_{\text{La}}$$ $$\Delta m = 57(1.00728) + 82(1.00863) - 138.955$$ $$\Delta m \approx 1.168\text{ u}$$ The nucleus is lighter than its parts. That lost mass holds the nucleus together.

Step 2: **Convert to Total Binding Energy**
Use $1\text{ u} = 934\text{ MeV}$: $$E_b = \Delta m \times 934$$ $$E_b = 1.16762 \times 934 \approx 1091\text{ MeV}$$

Step 3: **Share Per Nucleon**
Divide by the total number of nucleons, $A = 139$: $$\text{BE per nucleon} = \frac{1091}{139} \approx 7.85\text{ MeV}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: State and explain whether the binding energy per nucleon of uranium-235 ($^{235}_{92}\text{U}$) will be greater, equal to or less than your answer in (b)(ii).

markscheme_points.text: above $A = 56$, binding energy per nucleon decreases as $A$ increases
binding energy per nucleon less (for uranium than for products)

hints: Hint 1: Picture the shape of the binding energy per nucleon against mass number graph and recall where its peak lies near $A = 56$.
Hint 2: Compare the positions of La-139 ($A = 139$) and U-235 ($A = 235$) on that graph, both to the right of the peak.
Hint 3: Link the direction of the curve beyond the peak to fission: think why splitting a very heavy nucleus into medium nuclei releases energy.
parts.proper_answer: Less than in (b)(ii). Above $A \approx 56$ binding energy per nucleon decreases as $A$ increases, and U-235 has larger $A$ than La-139. Equivalently, fission of U-235 releases energy so products are more tightly bound per nucleon than uranium.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the BE Per Nucleon Curve**
Binding energy per nucleon is a measure of how tightly each nucleon is held. It rises to a maximum around iron with $A \approx 56$ and then slowly falls for heavier nuclei because the long-range repulsion between many protons starts to win over the short-range strong attraction.

Step 2: **Compare La-139 and U-235**
Both $A = 139$ and $A = 235$ lie on the falling part of the curve to the right of the peak. Since $235 > 139$, uranium sits further down the slope: $$\text{BE per nucleon (U-235)} < \text{BE per nucleon (La-139)}$$

Step 3: **See It Through Fission**
Another way to see the same physics is that uranium undergoes fission into lighter fragments like Mo and La plus energy. Energy can only come out if the products are more bound per nucleon than the parent, so the parent U-235 must have the smaller value, about $7.6\text{ MeV}$ compared with $7.85\text{ MeV}$ for La-139.
